context_blurb:
How fast is a bike, a bus or a storm going, and which way? Physics answers with three careful words: speed, velocity and acceleration. A tape measure and a stopwatch are enough to measure them, and a simple graph can turn a whole trip into one line you read at a glance.

Speed is how far something travels in a given time, in metres per second or kilometres per hour. A speedometer shows the speed at one instant. Average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time, and every minute counts, even minutes spent standing still. A walker who covers six kilometres in two hours averages three kilometres per hour; if she also rests for an hour, the same six kilometres take three hours, and her average falls to two. A rest adds time but no distance, so it always pulls the average speed below the speed shown while moving.

Velocity is speed together with a direction: thirty kilometres per hour toward the east is a velocity, while thirty kilometres per hour alone is only a speed. A weather report that gives a storm's speed but not which way it is heading cannot tell a town whether the storm will reach it at all. Distance is the whole length of a path. Displacement is the straight-line change of position from start to finish, and average velocity is worked out from it, not from the distance. A lap of a running track ends on the very line where it began, so its displacement is zero, and so is its average velocity, however fast the runner went.

A distance-time graph draws a trip as one line, with time running along the bottom and distance climbing up the side. To make one, mark a hallway with tape every metre, call out the seconds while a friend walks along it, and plot which mark the walker reaches at each call. The slope of the line, its steepness, is the speed: a steeper line gains more distance every second, and a straight line means a steady speed. So when two riders set off together and one rider's straight line climbs more steeply than the other's, the steeper line belongs to the faster rider. A flat stretch means the clock runs on while the distance stays the same, so the walker was standing still in one spot. A curved line means the speed is changing. A line that keeps rising but grows less and less steep shows something slowing down: it is still moving forward, but it covers less ground each second. And a graph is not a picture of the road: a steep line means fast, not uphill.

Two runners on one straight track make two lines, and when one starts ahead but the other runs faster, the lines cross. A crossing point marks a moment when both runners are the same distance from the start line, which means they are side by side. At a crossing the two lines have different slopes, and the steeper belongs to the runner who has caught up and is passing. In 1980 the researchers Trowbridge and McDermott found that students who compared two moving things wrongly nearly always did so by judging speed from position, as if being in the same place meant going at the same speed.

Acceleration is any change in velocity: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. In everyday speech, to accelerate means only to speed up, but science counts all three. So a cyclist braking for a red light is accelerating, because her speed is changing; her acceleration simply points backward, against her motion. Everyday speech calls that deceleration. A car rounding a curved road at one steady speed is accelerating too, because its direction, and so its velocity, keeps changing. Going fast is a different thing: a car holding one speed along a straight road has an unchanging velocity, so its acceleration is zero, however fast it goes.
